title: Utility-First Approach
definition: The core philosophy of building complex components from a constrained set of primitive utilities.
simpleExplanation: It feels incredibly wrong at first. Your HTML looks messy, crowded, and ugly with 15 classes on a single `div`. But after 2 days, you realize you can build an entire website 5x faster because you never have to switch tabs to a CSS file.
realWorldExample: Building a custom gradient button with hover states, focus rings, and dark mode support entirely inside a React component file.

basic: Why does Tailwind HTML look so crowded?
intermediate: Doesn't utility-first CSS violate the 'Separation of Concerns' principle?

answers.question: Crowded HTML?
answers.answer: Because you are composing complex designs using many tiny, single-purpose classes. (e.g., `flex`, `items-center`, `justify-between`, `p-4`).

answers.question: Separation of Concerns?
answers.answer: Historically, we separated HTML (Structure) and CSS (Style). However, modern frameworks like React proved that separating by Component (Structure + Style + Logic together) is vastly superior for maintainability.

codeExample:
<!-- This might look horrifying if you are used to traditional CSS... -->
<button class="bg-indigo-600 hover:bg-indigo-700 text-white font-semibold py-2 px-4 rounded-lg shadow-md focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 focus:ring-indigo-500 focus:ring-opacity-75 transition-colors duration-200">
  Save Changes
</button>

<!-- ...But it is incredibly maintainable because you know exactly what every class does, and deleting this button won't leave dead CSS code in your project! -->
